extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and cultural critics (Victorian/middle-class audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive criteria for assessing and advancing 'culture' (the ideal of harmonious human development), contrasting Hellenism (sweetness and light) with Hebraism (strictness of conscience) and advising how to balance them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness and light (Hellenism)
rubrics_metrics.description: To work for 'sweetness and light' — the Hellenic bent: the instinct for the true, firm, intelligible law of things; the love of light and of seeing things as they are; fidelity to nature and delicate discrimination of the best nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hellenism underlies Greek intelligence and art and is the source of scientific and aesthetic success; it demands that things be seen in truth and beauty. Examples: Greek art and Greek science as exemplars. Anti-patterns: fanatic hostility to moral strictness (an extreme Hellenism) which can lack sweetness and hence light. Use Hellenism to develop the intellectual and aesthetic side of humanity and to make other pursuits intelligible and beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strictness of conscience (Hebraism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebraism values obedience and the moral side of human nature — strictness of conscience and staunch adherence to fixed laws of doing — over intellectual spontaneity and freedom of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hebraism supplies moral earnestness and force but if excessive becomes mechanical and narrow (the 'one thing needful'), leading to vulgarity, ignorance, and a rigidity that misreads texts and ossifies practice. Examples of misapplied Hebraism include Puritanical readings of Scripture and social attitudes that treat rules as talismans. Assessments should note when moral earnestness crowds out fuller human development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonious, all-round development (culture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture aims at the 'full and harmonious development of our humanity' — to come to our best at all points, not to single out one side of human nature as sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions and institutions by whether they cultivate the whole person (moral, intellectual, aesthetic), not merely obedience or mere utility. Culture promotes spontaneity of consciousness and a free play of thought around practice. The pursuit of culture typically requires books, reading, observation and thought to approach the intelligible law of things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right reason as authoritative foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: Only in 'right reason' can one find a sure authority; culture brings us towards right reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value arguments, practices, and reforms that rest on reasoned understanding rather than on mere habit, dogma, or mechanical rule. Use culture (reading, thinking) to secure a rational basis for less confused action. Reject forms of authority that are merely ritualized or taken as absolute without reasoned comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity of consciousness / free play of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage letting 'consciousness play freely' around present operations and stock notions — a spontaneity of thought that tests, enlarges, and renews rules and habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer interpretations and practices that are fluid, contextual, and revisable rather than fixed and mechanical. Example: St. Paul's ethical teaching should be allowed to play in the mind, not be treated as static talismans. Methods: critical reflection, contextual reading, imaginative reapplication of received ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical/isolated interpretation of texts and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat writings or rules as absolutely final, fixed, or talismanic; avoid using terms in an 'isolated, fixed, mechanical way' rather than in their connected, fluid sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should prefer readings that seek the author's movement of ideas and original context. Anti-patterns include Puritanical slicing-off of terms (e.g., grace, faith, resurrection) into single static meanings; examples given: common postures toward St. Paul and the doctrine of resurrection. Scoring: interpretations that preserve nuance, historical context, and living application rate higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Import Hellenism into Hebraism (renewal of moral motive-power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revive and renew moral rules (Hebraism) by subjecting them to Hellenic free thought — a deliberate importation of intellectual freedom to reanimate petrified rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical remedy for mechanical religiosity: guide moral conscience by reflective reasoning and imaginative engagement. Example: St. Paul's method of exposing mechanical religion and recovering its living force. Policies or practices should be judged by whether they refresh moral motive-power rather than entrench mechanical adherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue social goods with reference to human perfection (avoid fetishizing means)
rubrics_metrics.description: When pursuing industrial enterprise, bodily exercises, and freedom, do so with constant reference to the ideal of complete human perfection rather than treating them as ends in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If industrial prowess, muscularity, or liberty are pursued mechanically as ends, they become mere 'machinery' or fetish and fail to inspire admiration. Compare British mechanical pursuit with Greek pursuit oriented to human perfection. Evaluate social practices on whether they are means toward harmonious development or isolated fetishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as integral to intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no intelligible law of things unless they are also beautiful; body, behaviour, discourse, song, and worship must satisfy the mind by being beautiful as well as true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess aesthetic and moral acts for whether they harmonize intelligibility and beauty. Anti-patterns: mean, vulgar, or hideous expressions that claim substance but lack aesthetic integrity; example criticisms include certain popular chapels, hymns, and public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fanaticism of either Hellenism or Hebraism
rubrics_metrics.description: Both sides have dangers: excessive Hebraism leads to mechanical, narrow, and crude life; excessive Hellenism risks moral relaxation and lack of earnestness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good cultural judgment balances the two impulses according to time and circumstances. Do not valorize one absolutely; weighting should depend on particular needs (e.g., some periods or persons may need more moral strictness, others more intellectual enlargement). Examples: Mr. Sidgwick's claim that 'the world wants fire and strength even more than sweetness and light' — correct emphasis is situational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pedantic/bookish culture while defending true culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is not mere bookishness or pedantry; the aim is the enabling of a nearer approach to the intelligible law of things, not an indulgence in scholarship for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique false culture (frivolous or pedantic) but avoid discrediting authentic culture that seeks human perfection. Practices should be evaluated on whether books and learning are used instrumentally to further whole-person development rather than as self-indulgent ends.
